tldr: The authors propose ARC, a bottom-up framework that delivers a withdrawal command to the motors within 10 ms before the initial impact peak arrives, while learning a whole-body control policy that maintains balance and enables long-horizon avoidance without canceling out the reflex. On a real humanoid robot, this cuts contact impulse in half and ensures safe task continuation.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of ARC (Ascending Reflex Control). Hazardous contact is detected within 5 ms of an impact, and a model-predictive optimization solver computes a whole-body withdrawal pose delivered directly to the motors within 10 ms. A high-level learned whole-body policy then seamlessly takes over without suppressing the reflex, safely withdrawing into a safe zone guided by human motion priors.
overview:
For humanoid robots collaborating with humans in cluttered environments or navigating complex terrains, dealing with unexpected collisions is a matter of survival. Adding a compliant, human-like skin layer delays the impact peak by tens of milliseconds. However, conventional reinforcement learning-based whole-body policies running at around 50 Hz miss this withdrawal window due to policy-cycle inference delays (up to 20 ms). Even worse, motion-tracking policies view abrupt postural disturbances as tracking errors, actively fighting to restore the original pose and canceling out the protective withdrawal.

To solve this, the authors drew inspiration from biological spinal reflex arcs and designed ARC (Ascending Reflex Control). ARC detects subtle contacts buried in vibration noise right at the start of a collision using 'tactile startle' detection across piezoresistive fabric tactile patches. A model-based optimization solver then computes a whole-body withdrawal pose and sends it directly to the motors within 10 ms of contact. To prevent the high-level policy from resisting the reflex, ARC introduces reflex-transparent policy alignment—which subtracts the reflex displacement from observations—and counterfactual imitation learning, letting the policy maintain balance without suppressing the reflex.

In hardware experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid, compared to an otherwise identical reflex delayed by just 20 ms, ARC reduced the first force peak by 34.1% and cut the contact impulse from 0.2632 Ns to 0.1225 Ns (a 2.15x reduction). The framework also proved effective in demanding real-world tasks, including tracking high-speed dance and kung-fu motions, teleoperation, and vision-free obstacle traversal guided by foot tactile sensing.
contributions: Built an instantaneous tactile reflex pipeline that detects hazardous contact in the very first frame and issues whole-body motor commands within 10 ms via model-based optimization.
Proposed a bottom-up reflex integration mechanism that keeps the high-level policy from canceling out reflex displacements as tracking errors, co-controlling the same joints for reflex and balance.
Incorporated human avoidance behaviors as motion priors (AMP) to naturally transition from an initial local reflex withdrawal into a global whole-body escape.

Demonstrated on a real Unitree G1 humanoid that a 20 ms delay increases contact impulse by 2.15x, and validated safe execution across challenging contact tasks including blind obstacle traversal and teleoperation.

sections.heading: Why humanoid reflexes demand a bottom-up approach
sections.summary: When humanoids work in real-world environments, impact peaks from unexpected collisions arrive within tens of milliseconds—far too fast for high-level policy inference cycles. Because whole-body policies also treat sudden reflex motions as disturbances and try to suppress them, a new architecture is needed to coordinate fast low-level reflexes with high-level balance control on the same joints.
sections.details:
When humanoid robots share space with humans or traverse unmapped terrain, unexpected contacts can damage the robot, harm people nearby, or cause the robot to fall. Adding a soft, compliant layer to the robot's surface delays the initial impact peak by tens of milliseconds. However, taking advantage of this narrow window exposes two fundamental barriers in traditional top-down whole-body control.

The first is the latency barrier. Typical RL-based whole-body controllers run at around $50\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz}$ (a 20 ms cycle). When a tactile event occurs, the robot must wait until the next inference step, missing the chance to withdraw before the impact peak. The second is control interference. Motion-tracking policies are trained to minimize tracking deviations from reference trajectories and are regularized via domain randomization to aggressively reject sudden external perturbations. As a result, the policy mistakes the reflex withdrawal motion for a massive tracking error and immediately fights back, trying to restore the original trajectory.

While a robotic manipulator can simply yield full authority to a low-level controller during a reflex, a bipedal humanoid will collapse if it stops maintaining balance during a withdrawal. Whether withdrawing the torso, a knee, or even a hand, whole-body coordination is required. In short, low-level reflexes and high-level policies must send commands to the exact same joints simultaneously. To address this, the authors propose ARC, combining an instantaneous tactile reflex that actuates motors within 10 ms with a bottom-up integration scheme that aligns reflexes with the learned policy.

sections.heading: From contacts as disturbances to coordinated reflex responses
sections.summary: Recent humanoid control relies heavily on imitation learning to track reference motions, treating contacts merely as disturbances to reject. Meanwhile, classical reflex controllers either disable high-level planners or apply only to simpler robots, leaving the integration of learning-based whole-body balance and high-speed reflexes on the same degrees of freedom largely unexplored.
sections.details:
### II-A Whole-Body Control under Contact
Modern humanoid whole-body control largely focuses on motion tracking—reproducing human motion capture data. Scaling up model capacity and training data has enabled zero-shot tracking of unseen motions, forming the backbone of modern teleoperation. However, these systems use top-down designs that do not anticipate physical contact. Domain randomization simply trains the policy to treat contact forces as disturbances to cancel out. While predictive vision-based methods can avoid obstacles before contact, they inherit substantial inference latency from perception to action, leaving them powerless against unexpected, high-speed impacts that have already occurred. ARC keeps the existing tracking policy at the task layer while asking a critical question: what can be done in the blind window between the moment of impact and the policy's first response?

### II-B Reflex Control in Robotics
The essence of reflex control is decoupling time-critical reactive loops from slower deliberative processes. Prominent examples include optical-flow collision avoidance inspired by insect escape responses and tactile safety shields for robot arms. In humanoids, systems like SafeFall switch to dedicated fall-arrest policies. However, prior methods either shut off the high-level controller entirely during the reflex or rely on classical controllers without learned whole-body policies. Yet humanoids need the whole-body coordination of learned policies precisely during a withdrawal to prevent falls. ARC sets itself apart by keeping both pathways continuously active on the same degrees of freedom and resolving their mutual interference by design.

captions.F2: Overview of the ARC control architecture. The Instantaneous Reflex pathway on the left performs local withdrawal within 10 ms of contact detection, while the Bottom-Up Reflex Integration pathway on the right reconciles the reflex with the high-level policy to sustain balance and achieve long-horizon escape.

sections.heading: Breaking the 10 ms barrier: tactile startle detection and whole-body optimization
sections.summary: By checking deviations from a baseline and evaluating spatial connectivity, ARC detects hazardous collisions in the very first tactile frame (within 5 ms). A local quadratic program (LQP) that accounts for whole-body inertia then computes a withdrawal pose that pins the stance feet and constrains horizontal CoM drift within 4 ms, sending commands straight to the motors.
sections.details:
### III-A Tactile Startle Detection
Piezoresistive fabric tactile patches were placed across the Unitree G1 (wrists, elbows, knees, chest, back, and insteps). Each $16\text{\,}\mathrm{cm}\times8\text{\,}\mathrm{cm}$ patch contains 128 sensing elements (taxels) streaming 8-bit pressure values at 300 Hz (a ~3.3 ms period). While standard tactile systems aggregate several frames to confirm stable contact patterns, withdrawing before the impact peak requires making a decision on the very first frame of contact.

Dynamic motions introduce baseline fabric deformation and vibration noise. The authors leveraged two key insights: (1) impact pressure forms spatially compact, connected clusters, whereas vibration noise is diffuse, and (2) elements that are quiet during regular motion suddenly activate upon impact. By setting adaptive thresholds based on nominal motion baselines, the system identifies activated taxels and groups them using connected-component labeling. The cluster's centroid and surface normal determine the contact point and withdrawal direction $\mathbf{n}$, triggering a reflex within 5 ms of contact.

### III-B Model-Based Instant Reflex Solver
Once contact is detected, the solver computes a withdrawal pose $\mathbf{q}_r$ (displacement $\Delta\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}_r - \mathbf{q}_0$) from the current joint angles $\mathbf{q}_0$. Single-link inverse kinematics used for arms cannot handle high-inertia segments like the torso or legs, and sudden center-of-mass (CoM) shifts will quickly topple a biped.

The authors formulated a constrained whole-body optimization problem with an objective penalizing insufficient withdrawal $E_{\mathrm{wd}}$, a directional cone alignment term $E_{\mathrm{dir}}$, joint limits, and self-collision constraints. Crucially, joint displacement costs are weighted by the whole-body inertia matrix evaluated at $\mathbf{q}_0$, naturally balancing high-inertia waist rotations against low-inertia wrist motions based on physical cost. Furthermore, horizontal CoM displacement is heavily penalized, while vertical CoM movement—such as extending a leg to escape a knee strike—is permitted via rank-1 substraction.

Linearizing this formulation into short iterations of a local quadratic program (LQP) yields a solution on onboard compute in under 4 ms. Combined with detection, ARC delivers joint targets directly to motor drives within 10 ms of impact.

captions.F3: Different whole-body withdrawal poses computed instantaneously from the same initial stance, depending on the contact location (right hand, right elbow, right knee, chest, left hand, left elbow, left knee, back) and impact direction. The solver pulls the contacted site away while pinning the feet and preserving horizontal CoM balance.

sections.heading: Hiding the reflex: bottom-up integration techniques
sections.summary: To stop the reflex from clashing with the high-level policy, the authors introduce three techniques: 'Reflex-in-the-Loop' training, 'Reflex-Transparent' alignment that offsets observations and actions to hide the reflex from the policy, and 'Reflex-Informed' adaptation that leverages human motion priors for long-horizon recovery.
sections.details:
### IV-A Reflex-in-the-Loop Policy Learning
To ensure the tracking policy stays stable when a reflex occurs, the low-level reflex was embedded directly into the PPO motion-tracking training loop. The state space was augmented with patch trigger flags, withdrawal directions, and the active $\Delta\mathbf{q}$, while the tracking reference during a reflex shifts to $\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{ref}} + \Delta\mathbf{q}$.

However, running the reflex naively inside a massively parallel simulation (4,096 environments in Isaac Lab) creates two problems: sparse contact events lead to sample inefficiency, and asynchronous LQP solver calls cause severe CPU bottlenecks. To solve this, the authors built 'ARC-Gym'. When a collision occurs during tracking iterations, the environment state is saved to a buffer and reset. At the end of the iteration, the LQP solver processes all buffered states in a single batch. The next training iteration loads these precomputed reflex trajectories across all environments simultaneously, enabling highly efficient recovery training.

### IV-B Reflex-Transparent Policy Alignment
When a reflex intervenes, the policy treats the resulting motion as tracking error and outputs opposing torques to cancel it out. The authors resolved this by placing the policy in a virtual world where the reflex never happened.

Specifically, the reflex displacement $\Delta\mathbf{q}$ is subtracted from the joint angles observed by the policy, and then added back to the policy's output PD targets before reaching the motors. As a result, the policy always sees observations drawn from its familiar non-reflex distribution. Because subtle dynamic changes could still allow the policy to learn indirect cancellation behaviors, the authors added a DAgger-style regularization loss $r_{\mathrm{tp}}$ pulling outputs toward the action that would be chosen in the counterfactual non-reflex state $\mathbf{s}^-$. This transparency mechanism drastically reduces policy learning complexity while allowing the reflex to act with 100% authority in the real world.

### IV-C Reflex-Informed Policy Adaptation
While a local reflex withdrawal takes only tens of milliseconds, kinematically pulling a limb back is rarely enough to clear an obstacle entirely due to joint limits and support foot constraints. The robot must step away and relocate its entire body over several seconds.

However, if the reference motion expects the robot to stay in place, simply granting freedom to deviate causes the humanoid to twist into awkward, unstable postures. To prevent this, the authors collected human motion capture data of stepping and turning away from obstacles, using it as an adversarial reward $r_{\mathrm{ad}}$ via Adversarial Motion Priors (AMP). This allows the policy to depart from the reference motion and step safely away from obstacles using natural, human-like gait patterns for long-horizon recovery.

captions.F4: Conceptual diagram of Reflex-Transparent Policy Alignment (One Mapping). Subtracting the reflex displacement from observations and adding it back to the policy outputs keeps the policy's input space within its nominal tracking distribution. DAgger-style regularization against counterfactual non-reflex states further suppresses unintended compensation.

sections.heading: Hardware trials: how a 20 ms delay doubles impact impulse
sections.summary: Impact experiments on a real Unitree G1 striking a rigid box demonstrated that adding a 20 ms delay increases contact impulse by 2.15x, confirming the value of a sub-10 ms response. The system reliably handled demanding tasks like martial arts tracking, teleoperation, and blind obstacle traversal, while ablations confirmed the necessity of each design component.
sections.details:
### V-A Quantitative Contact Impact Analysis
The authors evaluated arm strikes against a rigid box instrumented with tactile sensors, capturing impacts with a 240 Hz high-speed camera. They compared ARC against a baseline that applied the exact same reflex command delayed by 20 ms—the delay typical of waiting for a 50 Hz policy cycle.

ARC's instantaneous bottom-up reflex reduced the initial force peak by 34.1%, from $21.64\text{\,}\mathrm{N}$ down to $14.25\text{\,}\mathrm{N}$. More importantly, the total contact impulse (force integrated over time) was more than halved, dropping from $0.2632\text{\,}\mathrm{N}\cdot\mathrm{s}$ to $0.1225\text{\,}\mathrm{N}\cdot\mathrm{s}$—meaning a 20 ms delay caused a 2.15x surge in impulse. Without delay, the robot begins withdrawing during the early force ramp, shedding momentum before peak contact. With a delay, the limb only begins to move after its momentum has already been fully transferred into the obstacle.

### V-B Real-World Case Studies
ARC was evaluated on three demanding tasks using the real G1 humanoid:
- **Motion Tracking in Cluttered Scenes**: While tracking over 10 distinct dynamic motions (dancing, kung fu, marching), the robot was subjected to three hazard categories: (1) static obstacles, (2) dynamic projectiles like thrown objects, and (3) unexpected human contact. The robot withdrew instantly upon impact, mitigated peak forces, and sustained balance without interruption.
- **Protected Teleoperation**: In a teleoperated data collection setup driven by a foundation tracking model (ScaleBFM), the authors tested adding $\Delta\mathbf{q}$ directly into the reference trajectory. While functional, the tracking model's inference latency and smoothing bias noticeably slowed down the response compared to ARC's direct motor pathway.
- **Adaptive Locomotion (Blind Obstacle Traversal)**: Using tactile patches on the insteps, the robot negotiated obstacles without vision. When a foot struck a block, instead of merely pulling back, it lifted the foot up and forward to step over it. Simply reversing the long-horizon direction goal and providing human stepping demonstrations to AMP allowed the blind humanoid to recover from foot trips and clear raised thresholds.

### V-C Ablation Studies
Simulation ablations isolated the impact of each core component:
- **Without Reflex-in-the-Loop**: The policy could not handle post-reflex pose distributions; survival rates dropped to $82.0\%$, and obstacle re-hit rates jumped to $90.9\%$.
- **Without Adaptation**: Local withdrawals succeeded, but the robot remained stuck near the obstacle, causing an $88.0\%$ re-hit rate.
- **Without Transparency**: While avoidance metrics appeared fine superficially, the policy's compensation score $C$ turned positive ($+29.7$), revealing that the policy actively fought the reflex. This cut withdrawal distance from $11.06\text{\,}\mathrm{cm}$ to $6.74\text{\,}\mathrm{cm}$ and increased impulse from $3.42\text{\,}\mathrm{N}\cdot\mathrm{s}$ to $4.22\text{\,}\mathrm{N}\cdot\mathrm{s}$.
- **Explicit Trajectory Tracking (Without AMP)**: Replacing AMP with direct trajectory tracking caused the rate of escaping beyond 1.5 m to plummet from $63.0\%$ to $14.1\%$, with a $0\%$ success rate on climbing stairs or stepping over thresholds.

captions.F5: Real-world validation on the Unitree G1 humanoid. The robot swiftly pulls away from human touches and obstacle impacts while executing high-speed dance and martial arts motions, withstands thrown dynamic projectiles, and steps over thresholds and stairs blindly using foot tactile feedback.

sections.heading: Looking forward: toward seamless whole-body electronic skin
sections.summary: ARC establishes a bottom-up control paradigm that pairs sub-10 ms tactile reflexes with learned whole-body policies on shared joints, cutting impact impulse in half. Its primary limitation today is sensor coverage, making full-body electronic skin a key direction for future work.
sections.details:
This paper introduced ARC, a bottom-up humanoid control framework that allows model-based instantaneous tactile reflexes to share authority with learned whole-body tracking policies on identical degrees of freedom. By detecting contact in the very first tactile frame and resolving an inertia-aware LQP within 10 ms, ARC sharply suppresses early impact peaks. Through reflex-in-the-loop training, transparent observation/action alignment, and human motion priors (AMP), the framework prevents high-level policies from fighting the reflex, naturally bridging fast local reactions with stable, long-horizon escape steps.

The main limitation highlighted by the authors is tactile sensor coverage. Currently, patches are placed only on prominent, high-probability contact sites such as the wrists, elbows, knees, chest, back, and insteps. Contacts landing in uncovered gaps remain undetectable, leaving the robot vulnerable. Implementing seamless, high-density electronic artificial skin that covers the entire humanoid frame represents the most critical next step for this line of research.

takeaways: Beating the impact peak (tens of milliseconds) requires bypassing the 50 Hz high-level policy cycle and routing withdrawal commands directly to motors within 10 ms.
Because RL tracking policies naturally treat reflex displacements as tracking errors, making the reflex 'transparent' by offsetting observations and applying counterfactual losses is essential.
Local joint withdrawals cannot clear obstacles due to stance foot constraints, making multi-timescale integration with human motion priors (like AMP) critical for global escape.
When integrating heavy, asynchronous local optimization (LQPs) into parallel RL environments, buffering contact states for batch execution (the ARC-Gym pipeline) provides massive speedups.
limitations: Tactile patches are restricted to primary convex areas like wrists and knees, leaving the robot unprotected against unexpected collisions on unsensored surfaces.
LQP withdrawal generation relies on kinematic and inertial robot models; dynamic stability is not formally guaranteed under extreme, unknown external contact wrenches.
